stem: Urn I contains 3 red and 2 white balls. Urn II contains 1 red and 4 white balls. A fair coin is tossed. If heads, a ball is drawn from Urn I; if tails, from Urn II. The ball drawn is red. What is the probability that it came from Urn I?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Computing P(R|I)*P(I) = 3/5 * 1/2 = 3/10, then dividing by 1 (the full probability space) rather than P(R), giving 3/10 miswritten as 3/8.

Using P(R|I) / [P(R|I) + P(R|II)] = (3/5) / (3/5 + 1/5) = 3/4 correctly but then miscomputing: 3/5 / (4/5) = 3/4, but writing 2/3 by using only red ball counts 3/(3+1+1) = 3/5 and converting incorrectly.
Ignoring the differing red-ball proportions and simply returning the prior P(Urn I) = 1/2 without updating on the red observation.

explanation_sections.punchline: Equal coin-flip priors cancel out (both times 1/2), so the posterior ratio equals the ratio of the likelihoods: 3/5 vs 1/5, giving 3:1 odds and P(I|R) = 3/4.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify model: Bayes theorem with two urns as hypotheses, equal priors. Likelihoods: P(R|I) = 3/5, P(R|II) = 1/5. Since priors are equal, posterior ratio = likelihood ratio = 3:1. P(I|R) = 3/(3+1) = 3/4. Full calculation: P(R) = (3/5 + 1/5)/2 = 4/10. P(I|R) = (3/10)/(4/10) = 3/4.
explanation_sections.lesson: When priors are equal, Bayes posterior is just the likelihood proportion; the prior 1/2 factors cancel and you compare the urn compositions directly.
explanation_sections.timing: 75 seconds. With equal priors the calculation reduces to likelihood ratio. The trap is stopping at P(I) = 1/2 without updating on the red draw.
